subject: Immunology
vignette: An 11-year-old boy presents with 3 weeks of polyuria, polydipsia, and a 3 kg weight loss. He is thin and has acetone on his breath. Labs: random glucose 480 mg/dL, arterial pH 7.18, bicarbonate 12 mEq/L, and urine positive for ketones. His father notes that a paternal uncle and a cousin also have diabetes. Antibodies to glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD65) are strongly positive, and C-peptide is low.
question: What is the primary mechanism destroying his pancreatic beta cells?

options.text: Antibody-mediated complement destruction of beta cells mediated by GAD65 autoantibodies alone
Peripheral insulin resistance with compensatory beta-cell hypertrophy
Virally induced direct cytolysis of beta cells by enteroviruses
T cell-mediated autoimmune destruction of insulin-producing beta cells
A somatic mutation in the insulin receptor causing insulin resistance from birth

explanation_correct: Type 1 diabetes is a T cell-mediated autoimmune disease in which CD4+ and CD8+ T cells destroy pancreatic beta cells, leading to absolute insulin deficiency. Islet autoantibodies to GAD65, insulin, IA-2, and ZnT8 are markers of the disease process rather than the effector mechanism themselves. Genetic susceptibility at HLA-DR3 and HLA-DQ2/8 loci and environmental triggers contribute, and low C-peptide confirms near-complete beta-cell destruction. Absolute insulin deficiency permits ketogenesis, explaining his diabetic ketoacidosis.

explanation_incorrect.A: Autoantibodies such as anti-GAD65 serve as serologic markers of autoimmune insulitis; the destructive effector mechanism is T cell-mediated, not antibody and complement.
explanation_incorrect.B: Insulin resistance with compensatory hyperplasia describes type 2 diabetes, which is rare in a thin 11-year-old with ketoacidosis and positive autoantibodies.
explanation_incorrect.C: An enterovirus trigger has been proposed as an environmental factor, but direct cytolysis is not the established mechanism of beta-cell destruction.
explanation_incorrect.E: Insulin receptor mutations cause rare inherited insulin-resistant syndromes and do not produce autoantibody-positive ketoacidosis.

educationalObjective: Type 1 diabetes is caused by T cell-mediated autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells, with islet autoantibodies serving as markers of the disease process.

subject: Immunology
vignette: A 29-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes diagnosed at age 15 presents with fatigue, cold intolerance, and a swollen neck. Examination reveals a diffuse, nontender goiter. Labs: TSH 14 uIU/mL, free T4 low, anti-thyroid peroxidase antibodies positive, and HbA1c 8.9%. Over the past 2 years she has also reported dry mouth and fatigue, with a positive anti-tissue transglutaminase IgA antibody on screening, confirmed by duodenal biopsy. She asks why she needs screening for other diseases.
question: Which of the following best explains her development of these additional conditions?

options.text: Deficiency of AIRE protein causing failure to delete autoreactive T cells in the thymus
Autoimmune polyendocrine-type clustering due to shared HLA-DR3/DQ2 susceptibility genes and a common autoimmune diathesis
Hyperglycemia directly inducing autoimmune thyroiditis through advanced glycation end products
Loss of pancreatic beta cells releasing antigen that cross-reacts with thyroid tissue
Chronic insulin injections activating complement and causing bystander autoimmune activation

explanation_correct: Type 1 diabetes is part of the polyglandular autoimmune cluster that includes Hashimoto thyroiditis, celiac disease, Addison disease, and vitiligo. These conditions share HLA-DR3 and HLA-DQ2 haplotypes, which shape antigen presentation and create a common susceptibility to loss of tolerance to several tissues. Because of this, patients with type 1 diabetes should be screened for thyroid dysfunction (TSH) and celiac disease (tissue transglutaminase antibodies) at intervals. Her goiter, low free T4, high TSH, and anti-TPO antibodies confirm Hashimoto thyroiditis.

explanation_incorrect.A: Deficiency of AIRE causes the rare autoimmune polyendocrinopathy-candidiasis-ectodermal dystrophy (APECED) syndrome, which presents in childhood with mucocutaneous candidiasis and hypoparathyroidism.
explanation_incorrect.C: Chronic hyperglycemia does not induce autoimmune thyroiditis; shared immune susceptibility underlies their co-occurrence.
explanation_incorrect.D: Antigen cross-reactivity between beta cells and thyroid has not been established as the cause; HLA-based shared susceptibility is the accepted explanation.
explanation_incorrect.E: Exogenous insulin is not known to cause bystander autoimmune activation, and insulin autoantibodies occur during disease progression, not as the cause of other organ-specific autoimmunity.

educationalObjective: Type 1 diabetes is associated with other organ-specific autoimmune diseases through shared HLA susceptibility, warranting screening for thyroid disease and celiac disease.
